title: AnalogVerifier: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Analog Circuit Verification
one_liner: AnalogVerifier turns loose circuit specifications into ordered testbench tasks, then checks numbers and repairs failures with deterministic tools.
lead: Analog circuit verification is hard to automate because the specification is usually written in loose engineering language while the final testbench must obey exact signal dependencies and exact numeric limits. A plain language model struggles here because it can misread dependencies, mix up task order, or invent thresholds. AnalogVerifier splits the job into four smaller parts so the language model handles interpretation while symbolic tools handle ordering and exact numeric grounding.

problem.h2: Why analog verification resists plain language-model automation
paras: An analog verification spec may say things such as: sweep this input range, wait for settling, measure gain at this node, and reject the design if a voltage crosses a limit. Those instructions are spread across prose, tables, and domain conventions. A testbench generator has to convert them into an ordered executable plan.

That conversion is brittle because order matters. Some checks depend on earlier setup steps, some ports must be driven before others, and numeric limits must match the spec exactly. If a generated testbench gets even one dependency or threshold wrong, the run can fail or produce a misleading pass.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Let the language model break the spec into atomic tasks, then use symbolic scheduling, deterministic numeric grounding, and repair from simulation feedback so the final testbench obeys design rules.

panels.title: 1. The spec is loose and mixed
panels.viz_args: One requirement is in prose, another is in a table, a third is implied by design convention.
panels.caption: The input is easy for humans to read but not ready for direct execution.

panels.title: 2. Plain generation can misorder checks
panels.viz_args: Measure output before bias setup -> invalid testbench
panels.caption: A wrong order breaks the test because dependencies were not enforced.

panels.title: 3. Split the spec into atomic tasks
panels.viz_args: Set bias. Sweep input. Wait. Measure output. Compare to limit.
panels.caption: Smaller tasks are easier to schedule and verify.

panels.title: 4. Symbolic tools enforce order and numbers
panels.viz_args: Dependency graph orders tasks; oracle computes exact thresholds.
panels.caption: The strict parts move to deterministic tools because exactness matters there.

panels.title: 5. Simulation feedback repairs the result
panels.caption: A failed run exposes missing or wrong steps, and the system patches the testbench.

steps.b: Serialize the spec into atomic tasks
steps.text: The system breaks the mixed specification into small test actions so each requirement can be handled separately.
Task dependencies are written as a graph so the system can determine which signals and checks must happen before others.

steps.b: Ground numeric limits with a symbolic oracle
steps.text: Exact thresholds are computed by deterministic rules or calculators so the final testbench uses the correct values.

steps.b: Generate the testbench in the required order
steps.text: The ordered tasks are converted into executable verification code.
Simulation feedback reveals missing coverage or failing logic, and the system revises the testbench until it passes functional checks.

paras: The paper changes the path from specification text to final verification code. Instead of asking one model to do interpretation, ordering, arithmetic, and repair in a single pass, it assigns those roles to separate components because each part of the job needs a different kind of reliability.

hidden.name: Specification faithfulness
paras: Specification faithfulness asks whether the produced testbench still means the same thing as the original engineering spec. This quantity is hidden because a testbench may run without obvious errors while still checking the wrong order or the wrong numeric limit.

AnalogVerifier raises faithfulness by separating interpretation from enforcement. The language model proposes atomic tasks, but symbolic scheduling and deterministic threshold derivation constrain the output so the testbench stays closer to the source requirements.

heat.caption: Darker means the produced testbench is more likely to drift away from the source specification.

reads.html: This is the chance that the generated testbench is checking the right thing in the right order.

Faithfulness improves because the system turns prose into atomic tasks, enforces dependency order with a graph, derives exact thresholds with deterministic tools, and repairs using simulation feedback.

paras: The main gain comes from dividing the job by failure mode. Language models are useful for turning messy text into candidate tasks because they can read broad specification language. They are less trustworthy for strict ordering and exact numeric derivation. AnalogVerifier improves reliability by moving those strict parts to deterministic components.

Closed-loop repair adds a second gain because simulation gives concrete evidence about what is missing. If a testbench fails or lacks coverage, the repair step has a grounded signal to act on, so revisions are guided by execution results instead of guesswork.

stages.s: Break it into atomic verification tasks
Enforce task order with dependency rules
Ground exact numbers and run simulation
A more faithful testbench with repair feedback

items.html: If the first step breaks the spec into the wrong atomic tasks, later symbolic checks cannot fully recover because the meaning was already distorted.
If the dependency graph omits a real constraint, then the scheduler may produce an invalid order because it never knew that relation existed.
If simulation feedback is too coarse, the repair step may know that the testbench failed but not why, so the fix becomes harder to target.
The framework is most useful when specifications are heterogeneous and order-sensitive, because that is where symbolic enforcement and execution feedback add the most value.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a small analog component such as an amplifier with a short mixed-format spec. Build two pipelines: one plain text-to-testbench generator and one staged pipeline with task serialization, dependency scheduling, exact threshold grounding, and repair after simulation. Compare pass rate, number of manual edits, and coverage of required checks. The demo should show that the staged system produces more faithful testbenches because the strict parts of the job are enforced by deterministic tools.
demo.metric_eq: pass_rate = passing_testbenches / total_testbenches ; repair_load = manual_edits / total_testbenches
demo.closing: The demo must show fewer manual fixes and more correct end-to-end verification runs.
